# Written constitution (`written_constitution`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: needs writing_invention; helped by rule_of_law, representative_government, printing_press
- Core idea: One public document, adopted by a special procedure, states who holds which power, how office-holders are chosen and removed, and what government may never do. It ranks above ordinary law and can be changed only by a harder procedure than ordinary law, so that a passing majority or a ruler cannot rewrite the rules for itself. Because everyone can read the same text, everyone can see when it is broken, which lets opponents coordinate resistance. Keep it short: organs, their powers, terms, a list of rights, and the amendment rule.
- Pitfalls:
  - Believing the paper does the work: most constitutions ever written were ignored within a generation; it needs courts, an assembly and armed forces that obey it
  - Making it impossible to amend (it gets broken instead) or as easy as ordinary law (it protects nothing)
  - Calling older documents constitutions: Shotoku's 17 articles (604) are moral maxims and Magna Carta a list of baronial grievances
  - Letting the sitting ruler or assembly write it: a body that drafts its own powers takes too many; use a separate convention and ratification
- History: greece: 4th c. BC – Aristotle's school compiles descriptions of 158 city constitutions; a city's 'constitution' meant its arrangement of offices, not one document; islamic: c. 622 – the so-called Constitution of Medina, a written pact between the Muslim emigrants, the clans of Medina and Jewish groups (text in Ibn Ishaq; generally accepted as authentic, unity and date of its parts disputed); 1861 Tunisia; 1876 Ottoman constitution; east_asia: 604 – Shotoku's Seventeen Articles in Japan, ethical precepts for officials; 1889 Meiji Constitution; europe: 1600 – statutes of San Marino; 1634 Swedish Instrument of Government; 1653 Cromwell's Instrument of Government; 1755 Corsica (Paoli); 1791 Poland (3 May) and France; americas: 1639 – Fundamental Orders of Connecticut; 1776 US state constitutions; 1780 Massachusetts, drafted by a convention and ratified by the towns; 1787 US Constitution; 1805 Haiti; africa: 1847 – Liberia; the Manden Charter attributed to 1236 is oral tradition first written down in the 20th c.; india: 1950 – Constitution of India, the longest national constitution
- Read:
  - Hamilton, Madison & Jay, The Federalist Papers (1788)
